newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Big deals elusive at Abu Dhabi arms bazaar.
newsitem.headline: Big deals elusive at Abu Dhabi arms bazaar.

text.p: After five days of high hopes at Abu Dhabi's IDEX arms bazaar, big deals remained elusive and Washington appeared to lose ground to European competitors in a $6 billion race to sell warplanes to the United Arab Emirates.

"It was a big disappointment. Nothing happened," said a U.S. arms executive of the International Defence Exhibition, one of the biggest in the world, that ended on Thursday in the capital of the UAE, a prized player in the arms market.
The Americans had good reason to be upset.

Abu Dhabi announced during IDEX that the Eurofighter had re-entered a contest to sell the UAE up to 80 warplanes, competing with original favourites U.S. firm Lockheed Martin and France's Dassault Aviation.

Industry sources and diplomats had predicted that Lockheed Martin could win the bulk of the deal, while Washington was banking on pro-American sympathy from the Gulf War to help it secure a substantial package.

Colonel Obeid al-Kitbi, the UAE's deputy director-general of arms procurement, told a news conference that Abu Dhabi was having some technical problems with Lockheed and suggested that Dassault's new offer was attractive.
"The Americans are very upset with this move. They have been negotiating with the UAE for years and now they are wondering how long this will last," said a Western diplomat.
Lockheed Martin officials put on a brave face.
"It's the UAE's decision to make. The competition is still open. We are in this for the long haul," said spokesman Keith Mordoff.

Lockheed officials told Reuters this week that the U.S. government had approved almost all of the UAE's weaponry and technology requirements for the F-16 fighters it was seeking to sell Abu Dhabi, a move seen as a boost to the firm.
But Western diplomats and industry officials said that the UAE's decision to consider a new Eurofighter proposal might have been political.

"The UAE and the United States are close. UAE nationals send their kids to American schools but they are opposed to U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East. They see the Americans as biased (in favour of Israel)," said the Western diplomat.
Some industry officials agreed.
"I don't believe the problem is just technical," said one. "This may have been a slap on the hands of the Americans."
When asked if the dispute with Lockheed was connected to political differences with the U.S. government, Kitbi insisted the problem was merely technical. But he refused to elaborate.
Israel has expressed concern about a possible U.S. deal to sell up to 100 Lockheed F-16s in a multi-billion dollar deal to Saudi Arabia.

Over 750 companies and more than 50 defence ministers attended the IDEX show, but the deals announced seemed trivial compared to the contest to win business in Abu Dhabi, including the plane deal and a missile package.
The UAE said it had signed contracts ranging from a $75 million deal to buy 136 armoured combat vehicles from Turkish firm FMC-Nurol to a $4 million training contract for nurses of the armed forces.
As the show wound up, international firms were reminded that selling arms to Abu Dhabi was far tougher than setting up stands with high-tech weapons.
The UAE said on Wednesday it would halt business with a country's arms exporters if one of the country's firms reneged on agreements with Abu Dhabi.

A day earlier, it decided to halt deals with any Italian military firm after it failed to resolve a three-year-old dispute over a rapid launcher rocket system supplied by Italy's BPD Difesa e Spazio (Fiat Avio Group).
